notes: C1 reuses forcedAutomatedNames to add the names to the automate loader and builds a base policy with an internal split, so the main example matches the dummy-site output. It always emits a policy even with no global defaults, which adds noise and likely breaks exact adapt output. Its wildcard/catch-all-aware 'covered' check skips every name when a hostless site block exists, so internal names like localhost would lose the internal issuer. The refactor of existing split code into a helper drops warnings because the slice is passed by value.

Reuses forcedAutomatedNames and pulls the internal/public split into a shared helper, which is reasonable, but it detects 'already covered' with automationPolicyIsSubset, so a hostless or wildcard site-block policy swallows the listed names and they get no policy of their own; it also always creates a base policy (empty noise) and refactors existing site-block code, and its output diverges from the reference (hidden test fails).

C2 adds the names to the automate loader regardless of auto_https and validates them up front. It uses an exact-match check against existing policies, as the reference does, and splits internal names to the internal issuer. However, it copy-pastes the split logic, sorts the user's names, and always creates a policy even without global ACME defaults, so the noise policy diverges from the expected adapt output.

Parses the option correctly, adds the names to the automate loader, and leaves an existing site-block policy alone via an exact subject match; but it always creates a base policy even with no global options, which emits empty noise policies alongside other policies, and it sorts names and duplicates the site-block internal/public split inline, so its output diverges from the reference (hidden test fails).
